results.result: The authors developed fDNC, a transformer-based neural network trained on semi-synthetic data to find neural correspondence in C. elegans. The model is trained once on 2.304×10^5 semi-synthetic individuals generated by a simulator that applies transformations, noise, and variability to real neural configurations. The same pre-trained model can both track neurons within an individual across time and identify corresponding neurons across individuals.
results.evaluation: The methodological claims are well-documented with specific architectural details (C4, C33, C129-C133), training procedures (C5, C137-C141), and simulator specifications (C115, C119-C124). The semi-synthetic training approach is clearly described (C26-C31) with quantitative parameters. The transformer architecture choice is justified (C33-C35, C112-C113), and implementation details are provided (C125-C127, C136).

results.result: On held-out semi-synthetic test data, fDNC achieved 96.5% mean accuracy compared to CPD's 31.1% accuracy, demonstrating that fDNC significantly outperforms the baseline registration method on simulated data.
results.evaluation: The performance metrics on semi-synthetic data are clearly stated (C42, C43) with appropriate comparison to a baseline method (C44). The test set was properly held out from training (C41). However, high performance on semi-synthetic data does not guarantee similar performance on real data, which is appropriately evaluated separately in subsequent results.

results.result: fDNC achieves 79.1% accuracy at tracking neurons within a freely moving individual across time on real experimental data from Nguyen et al., 2017, significantly outperforming CPD (62.7%, p=2.5×10^-223) and the restricted NeRVE method (73.1%, p=1.3×10^-140), though slightly underperforming the full NeRVE method with 100 templates (82.9%, p=1.5×10^-102).
results.evaluation: The within-individual tracking performance is rigorously evaluated on real data with human-annotated ground truth (C45, C47). Statistical significance is properly reported (C49). The comparison to NeRVE is fair, acknowledging that NeRVE(100) uses additional information (C50). The biological validation with AVAL/AVAR calcium transients (C55) provides functional confirmation. The time-independent nature of the algorithms is correctly noted (C53-C54).

results.result: Using only position information, fDNC achieves 64.1% accuracy at identifying neurons across individuals on NeuroPAL data, with 76.6% accuracy when considering the top three candidate matches. The model was properly blinded to color information during evaluation.
results.evaluation: The across-individual performance is evaluated on properly held-out NeuroPAL data (C66) with human-annotated ground truth (C63, C65). The experimental design properly blinds the model to color information (C64), ensuring position-only evaluation. The top-3 accuracy metric (C70) provides useful additional information about model confidence. However, only 43% of neurons could be confidently labeled by humans (C65), which limits the evaluation scope.

results.result: When applied to an independent published dataset from Chaudhary et al., 2021, fDNC achieved 78.2% accuracy (91.3% top-3 accuracy) using only position information, outperforming CPD (58.9%) and demonstrating generalization to different imaging conditions and hardware without additional training.
results.evaluation: The validation on an independent dataset from a different group (C71, C99) provides strong evidence of generalization. The higher performance on this external dataset compared to the authors' own dataset (C73) suggests robustness. Statistical significance is reported (C71). The lack of additional training (C99) demonstrates true generalization rather than overfitting to specific conditions.

results.result: fDNC's accuracy (78%) is comparable to or better than the CRF method's open atlas variant (~40%) and comparable to the data-driven atlas variant (74%) on the Chaudhary et al., 2021 dataset, while offering advantages in speed and not requiring coordinate system transformation or a pre-assembled ground-truth atlas.
results.evaluation: The comparison to CRF is complicated by fundamental methodological differences (C75) that make direct accuracy comparison challenging. The authors acknowledge requiring assumptions to compare metrics (as noted in Table 2 discussion). While fDNC appears favorable, the comparison involves uncertainties about how unlabeled neurons affect the denominator. The claimed advantages (C78-C79) are valid, but the accuracy comparison itself (C76-C77, C80) requires assumptions that cannot be fully verified.

results.result: Adding a simple color model to fDNC increases accuracy from 64.1% to 74.7% on the authors' NeuroPAL dataset (92.4% top-3 accuracy). The framework can flexibly integrate additional features, and performance would likely improve further with more sophisticated color models.
results.evaluation: The improvement from adding color information is clearly demonstrated (C81-C82) with consistent improvement across all recordings (C82). The color model implementation is described (C145-C146). The comparison to Yemini et al., 2021 (C85-C86) appropriately contextualizes performance: fDNC performs better with position alone (64% vs 50%) but the sophisticated color model in Yemini performs better overall (86% vs 75%). The framework's flexibility (C87, C96) is demonstrated. The expectation of further improvement (C84, C97) is reasonable speculation.

results.result: fDNC predicts neural correspondence in 10 ms on GPU (50 ms on CPU), which is 93× faster than CPD (930 ms) and >1000× faster than NeRVE (>10 s). This speed of 100 volumes/second is an order of magnitude faster than typical imaging rates (6-10 volumes/second), making it suitable for future real-time applications, though fast segmentation algorithms would also be needed for complete closed-loop systems.
results.evaluation: The timing measurements are specific and compared on the same hardware (C56-C59). The speed advantage is substantial and well-documented. The comparison to imaging rates (C60) appropriately contextualizes the speed. The acknowledgment that fast segmentation is also needed (C61, C110) is honest about system requirements. The parallelization capabilities are explained (C149-C152). The claim about suitability for real-time applications (C13, C108) is appropriately qualified as future potential rather than current capability.

results.result: Unlike previous methods that require straightening or transforming the worm into a canonical coordinate system, fDNC finds neural correspondence directly from position information even when worms are in different poses or orientations, eliminating an error-prone preprocessing step.
results.evaluation: The claim is supported by citations showing that existing methods require straightening (C37) and by noting the difficulty of this task (C38). The transformer architecture's ability to handle different poses is demonstrated empirically through the performance results on real data with varying poses. However, it's worth noting that the simulator itself uses straightening as an intermediate step (C119), though the trained model does not require it.

results.result: fDNC's accuracy is comparable or favorable to other methods, though a theoretical upper bound may exist due to developmental variability. The 79% within-individual accuracy suggests room for improvement, and even 64% across-individual accuracy is sufficient for rejecting null hypotheses about stereotyped neural coding.
results.evaluation: The summary of comparative performance (C88) is supported by the detailed results. The discussion of theoretical limits (C89-C91) is appropriately speculative and acknowledges uncertainty. The reasoning about within-individual performance (C92-C93) is logical. The suggestion for improvement (C94) is reasonable. The claim about scientific utility at current accuracy levels (C95) is a valid assessment of practical value.

results.result: The fDNC framework offers multiple advantages: versatility (same model for within- and across-individual correspondence), generalization to different datasets, probability estimates for alternative matches, training without experimental ground truth, and GPU parallelization for speed.
results.evaluation: Each claimed advantage is supported by empirical results: versatility (C98) is demonstrated by performance on both tasks; probability estimates (C101-C102) are shown through top-3 accuracy metrics; training without ground truth (C106) is demonstrated by the semi-synthetic approach; GPU parallelization (C114) is shown by timing results. These are legitimate advantages over existing methods.

results.result: The manuscript provides appropriate background on C. elegans neuroscience, existing methods for neural correspondence, and the challenges of acquiring ground truth data, establishing the motivation for developing fDNC.
results.evaluation: The background claims are well-supported by appropriate citations (C1, C3, C14-C22, C32) and represent accurate characterizations of the field. The assessment of challenges (C2, C23-C25, C105) appropriately motivates the work. These are standard background claims that establish context.
